<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

steps.message: Validation accuracy rises from 93.85% to 95.41%, then falls to 90.04%. The records show both more missing boxed answers and more incorrect valid answers. I’ll write the report with the source-level defect, evidence that updates remain numerically stable, and the limits on linking the defect to those trends.

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch
*** Add File: /logs/artifacts/agent_answer.md
+# Diagnosis
+
+**The training computation is numerically stable but mathematically incorrect.** The principal defect is a silent target-alignment error in Qwen3-VL's Torch fused log-probability path with Ulysses sequence parallelism: hidden states are sequence-sharded, but the next-token targets supplied to the fused head are not. With SP2, the second sequence shard is scored and differentiated against targets from the first shard. High rewards, finite gradients, and successful completion do not establish correct GRPO optimization.
+
+## Source Evidence and Mechanism
+
+The recorded configuration activates this exact combination: four-way FSDP, SP2, remove-padding, Torch fused kernels, and the new worker implementation ([recorded-resolved.yaml:24](/workspace/config/recorded-resolved.yaml:24), [model settings:382](/workspace/config/recorded-resolved.yaml:382), [worker selection:831](/workspace/config/recorded-resolved.yaml:831)). The console confirms both Ulysses input slicing and the Torch fused backend on the actual workers ([console.log:862](/workspace/logs/console.log:862)). This is the engine path selected by [main_ppo.py:129](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/main_ppo.py:129), not the legacy `dp_actor.py` implementation.
+
+1. [FSDPEngineWithLMHead.prepare_model_inputs:924](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:924) correctly rolls the complete unpadded token sequence to construct next-token targets. For a VLM, it pads but retains the full input IDs so visual embeddings can be inserted before sequence slicing. It separately pads and SP-slices the rolled targets at line 943, storing them in `output_args`.
+2. [patch_vlm_for_ulysses_input_slicing:179](/workspace/framework/verl/models/transformers/monkey_patch.py:179) slices embeddings, position IDs, and visual inputs for the language model. Its returned hidden states therefore cover only the local sequence shard.
+3. The engine passes no labels to the fused forward ([transformer_impl.py:962](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:962), [extra arguments:1012](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:1012)). Consequently, [qwen3_vl.forward_with_torch_backend:287](/workspace/framework/verl/models/transformers/qwen3_vl.py:287) rolls the full input IDs and sends those full targets alongside the local hidden states to `FusedLinearForPPO`, without slicing targets by SP rank.
+4. [FusedLinearForPPOFunction.forward:99](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:99) checks target dimensionality but not matching token counts. It sets `T` from the local hidden-state length and takes target chunks starting at zero through `T`. Thus every SP rank consumes the target prefix. Backward uses those same incorrect targets ([torch_functional.py:181](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:181)). The returned local output length is valid, so gathering and unpadding do not detect the error.
+
+For example, take full IDs `[0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7]`. The globally shifted targets are `[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,0]`. SP rank 0 correctly consumes `[1,2,3,4]`; rank 1 should consume `[5,6,7,0]`, but also consumes `[1,2,3,4]`. This affects the second half of packed positions, including response positions, rather than merely a shard-boundary token. Coincidentally identical token IDs can conceal individual mismatches.
+
+I verified the failure with a small CPU algebra check using the supplied `FusedLinearForPPO`, random hidden states and vocabulary weights, and the Torch fallback for cross-entropy. Both ranks returned finite, correctly sized outputs. Rank 0 matched direct log-softmax/gather; rank 1's maximum absolute log-probability error was **2.300806** and hidden-gradient error was **4.424474**. This check loaded no model and performed no optimizer update or additional training.
+
+## Effect on GRPO
+
+The fused outputs bypass the engine's correctly sliced target tensor; the non-fused path actually uses it ([transformer_impl.py:1037](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:1037)). Both recomputed `old_log_probs` and differentiable current log-probabilities use the actor engine ([engine_workers.py:638](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine_workers.py:638)). GRPO's response advantages are therefore applied partly to probabilities of unrelated tokens, producing incorrect policy gradients. Using the same faulty code for old and current probabilities does not repair the action-gradient mismatch.
+
+The error also makes scores depend on packing: changing packed neighbors or a token's SP shard can change its target even with fixed model weights. Old-probability inference and minibatch updates can pack differently because updates first split the rollout batch and then dynamically form microbatches ([engine_workers.py:263](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine_workers.py:263), [engine/utils.py:74](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/utils.py:74)). Consequently, PPO ratios and clipping can also compare inconsistent target probabilities.
+
+`actor/ppo_kl` is the masked mean of `old_log_prob - log_prob`, after clamping their difference, not KL against the original reference model ([core_algos.py:1329](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:1329)). Its recorded range, **0.1177-0.5934**, and nonzero clipping are compatible with the defect but do not independently prove it: these metrics aggregate within-step optimization as well. Both reference-KL mechanisms are disabled, so the absence of a reference model is intentional.
+
+## What the Recording Shows
+
+[scalars.jsonl](/workspace/logs/scalars.jsonl) contains baseline validation and all 40 outer training steps. All recorded numeric scalars are finite. Policy loss ranges from **0.0844 to 0.3156**, gradient norm from **0.4003 to 4.0699**, and learning rate remains **1e-6**. There are no logged non-finite-gradient warnings, aborts, or prompt clipping. Gradient norms above 1 are not a clipping failure: the implementation reports the norm **before** clipping ([transformer_impl.py:635](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:635)). The stop at 40 is deliberate (`BENCH_STAGE_FINAL_STEP=40`, [console.log:2291](/workspace/logs/console.log:2291)); 200 is the configured training horizon, not evidence of an unexpected crash.
+
+The reward function awards exactly 1 for a correct final boxed option and 0 otherwise; `format_correct` is diagnostic, not an extra reward ([reward.py:4](/workspace/scripts/reward.py:4)). Logged scores and rewards agree throughout. Training reward is high but fluctuating: **0.9277** at step 1, a maximum of **0.9834** at step 9, and **0.9150** at step 40. The first-ten-step average is **0.9474**, versus **0.9163** over the last ten. This is not sustained reward improvement.
+
+GRPO's group normalization itself follows the expected UID-based computation ([core_algos.py:304](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:304), [ray_trainer.py:188](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/ppo/ray_trainer.py:188)). Homogeneous reward groups yield zero advantages; mixed groups provide signal. The observed extrema near **+/-2.47487** are consistent with eight-sample binary-reward groups. A negative token-averaged advantage or positive policy loss alone is not evidence of a sign error because response lengths weight the logged averages.
+
+Validation uses one sampled response per question, temperature 1 and top-p 0.7 ([recorded-resolved.yaml:270](/workspace/config/recorded-resolved.yaml:270)); training uses eight samples and top-p 1. The 1,024 validation questions and ground truths match across checkpoints. The scalar history and saved responses give:
+
+| Step | Validation Accuracy | Valid Boxed Answer |
+| --- | ---: | ---: |
+| 0 | 93.85% | 96.88% |
+| 5 | 95.02% | 98.63% |
+| 10 | 95.41% | 98.54% |
+| 15 | 94.92% | 97.95% |
+| 20 | 92.97% | 96.39% |
+| 25 | 91.50% | 95.90% |
+| 30 | 91.21% | 95.21% |
+| 35 | 90.63% | 95.12% |
+| 40 | 90.04% | 94.63% |
+
+The final accuracy is **3.81 percentage points below baseline** and **5.37 points below the step-10 peak**. Recounting the validation files gives 961 correct, 32 missing boxes, and 31 valid-but-wrong answers initially; finally, 922 correct, 55 missing boxes, and 47 valid-but-wrong answers. Thus both answer completion/format and answer correctness deteriorate. Re-extracting the last boxed option reproduces the saved scores at steps 0, 10, and 40.
+
+The response records also show repetitive unfinished answers, for example [40.jsonl:44](/workspace/logs/validation/40.jsonl:44), which repeatedly revisits the Massachusetts map question and never boxes an answer. Training's 4,096-token limit-hit rate rises from **0.78%** at step 1 to **5.37%** at step 40; its first-ten versus last-ten averages are **0.43% versus 4.67%**. Logged entropy falls from **0.4267 to 0.1257**, consistent with increasing concentration and repetitive behavior. Entropy is computed independently of the selected target IDs, so this remains useful observational evidence ([torch_functional.py:37](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:37)).
+
+The target defect establishes incorrect computation independently of these performance trends. The early validation improvement does not validate the implementation, and the later decline does not by itself diagnose it. The decline is consistent with corrupted policy updates, but this single sampled run cannot quantify the bug's causal contribution or exclude optimization effects from zero entropy regularization, no reference-KL penalty, and sparse mixed-group advantages.
+
+## Corrective Direction
+
+Before interpreting this recipe as a valid GRPO experiment, align fused targets with each local hidden-state shard: globally shift the unpadded IDs, apply the same padding and SP slicing, and consume those targets without shifting them again. The engine already constructs this tensor. Add an exact token-shape assertion in the fused head. Simply rolling an already sliced shard would introduce a boundary error. Disabling fused kernels consistently in the model and actor path is the immediate workaround because the non-fused engine uses the correct local targets. Verify fused/non-fused log-probability and gradient agreement under SP1 and SP2, including odd lengths and different packings. No training rerun was performed for this diagnosis.
*** End Patch"));

+2. [patch_vlm_for_ulysses_input_slicing:179](/workspace/framework/verl/models/transformers/monkey_patch.py:179) slices embeddings, position IDs, and visual inputs for the language model. Its returned hidden states therefore cover only the local sequence shard.
+3. The engine passes no labels to the fused forward ([transformer_impl.py:962](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:962), [extra arguments:1012](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:1012)). Consequently, [qwen3_vl.forward_with_torch_backend:287](/workspace/framework/verl/models/transformers/qwen3_vl.py:287) rolls the full input IDs and sends those full targets alongside the local hidden states to `FusedLinearForPPO`, without slicing targets by SP rank.
+4. [FusedLinearForPPOFunction.forward:99](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:99) checks target dimensionality but not matching token counts. It sets `T` from the local hidden-state length and takes target chunks starting at zero through `T`. Thus every SP rank consumes the target prefix. Backward uses those same incorrect targets ([torch_functional.py:181](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:181)). The returned local output length is valid, so gathering and unpadding do not detect the error.
+
+For example, take full IDs `[0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7]`. The globally shifted targets are `[1,2,3,4,5,6,7,0]`. SP rank 0 correctly consumes `[1,2,3,4]`; rank 1 should consume `[5,6,7,0]`, but also consumes `[1,2,3,4]`. This affects the second half of packed positions, including response positions, rather than merely a shard-boundary token. Coincidentally identical token IDs can conceal individual mismatches.
+
+I verified the failure with a small CPU algebra check using the supplied `FusedLinearForPPO`, random hidden states and vocabulary weights, and the Torch fallback for cross-entropy. Both ranks returned finite, correctly sized outputs. Rank 0 matched direct log-softmax/gather; rank 1's maximum absolute log-probability error was **2.300806** and hidden-gradient error was **4.424474**. This check loaded no model and performed no optimizer update or additional training.
+
+## Effect on GRPO
+
+The fused outputs bypass the engine's correctly sliced target tensor; the non-fused path actually uses it ([transformer_impl.py:1037](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:1037)). Both recomputed `old_log_probs` and differentiable current log-probabilities use the actor engine ([engine_workers.py:638](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine_workers.py:638)). GRPO's response advantages are therefore applied partly to probabilities of unrelated tokens, producing incorrect policy gradients. Using the same faulty code for old and current probabilities does not repair the action-gradient mismatch.
+
+The error also makes scores depend on packing: changing packed neighbors or a token's SP shard can change its target even with fixed model weights. Old-probability inference and minibatch updates can pack differently because updates first split the rollout batch and then dynamically form microbatches ([engine_workers.py:263](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine_workers.py:263), [engine/utils.py:74](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/utils.py:74)). Consequently, PPO ratios and clipping can also compare inconsistent target probabilities.
+
+`actor/ppo_kl` is the masked mean of `old_log_prob - log_prob`, after clamping their difference, not KL against the original reference model ([core_algos.py:1329](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:1329)). Its recorded range, **0.1177-0.5934**, and nonzero clipping are compatible with the defect but do not independently prove it: these metrics aggregate within-step optimization as well. Both reference-KL mechanisms are disabled, so the absence of a reference model is intentional.
+
+## What the Recording Shows
+
+[scalars.jsonl](/workspace/logs/scalars.jsonl) contains baseline validation and all 40 outer training steps. All recorded numeric scalars are finite. Policy loss ranges from **0.0844 to 0.3156**, gradient norm from **0.4003 to 4.0699**, and learning rate remains **1e-6**. There are no logged non-finite-gradient warnings, aborts, or prompt clipping. Gradient norms above 1 are not a clipping failure: the implementation reports the norm **before** clipping ([transformer_impl.py:635](/workspace/framework/verl/workers/engine/fsdp/transformer_impl.py:635)). The stop at 40 is deliberate (`BENCH_STAGE_FINAL_STEP=40`, [console.log:2291](/workspace/logs/console.log:2291)); 200 is the configured training horizon, not evidence of an unexpected crash.
+
+The reward function awards exactly 1 for a correct final boxed option and 0 otherwise; `format_correct` is diagnostic, not an extra reward ([reward.py:4](/workspace/scripts/reward.py:4)). Logged scores and rewards agree throughout. Training reward is high but fluctuating: **0.9277** at step 1, a maximum of **0.9834** at step 9, and **0.9150** at step 40. The first-ten-step average is **0.9474**, versus **0.9163** over the last ten. This is not sustained reward improvement.
+
+GRPO's group normalization itself follows the expected UID-based computation ([core_algos.py:304](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:304), [ray_trainer.py:188](/workspace/framework/verl/trainer/ppo/ray_trainer.py:188)). Homogeneous reward groups yield zero advantages; mixed groups provide signal. The observed extrema near **+/-2.47487** are consistent with eight-sample binary-reward groups. A negative token-averaged advantage or positive policy loss alone is not evidence of a sign error because response lengths weight the logged averages.
+
+Validation uses one sampled response per question, temperature 1 and top-p 0.7 ([recorded-resolved.yaml:270](/workspace/config/recorded-resolved.yaml:270)); training uses eight samples and top-p 1. The 1,024 validation questions and ground truths match across checkpoints. The scalar history and saved responses give:
+
+| Step | Validation Accuracy | Valid Boxed Answer |
+| --- | ---: | ---: |
+| 0 | 93.85% | 96.88% |
+| 5 | 95.02% | 98.63% |
+| 10 | 95.41% | 98.54% |
+| 15 | 94.92% | 97.95% |
+| 20 | 92.97% | 96.39% |
+| 25 | 91.50% | 95.90% |
+| 30 | 91.21% | 95.21% |
+| 35 | 90.63% | 95.12% |
+| 40 | 90.04% | 94.63% |
+
+The final accuracy is **3.81 percentage points below baseline** and **5.37 points below the step-10 peak**. Recounting the validation files gives 961 correct, 32 missing boxes, and 31 valid-but-wrong answers initially; finally, 922 correct, 55 missing boxes, and 47 valid-but-wrong answers. Thus both answer completion/format and answer correctness deteriorate. Re-extracting the last boxed option reproduces the saved scores at steps 0, 10, and 40.
+
+The response records also show repetitive unfinished answers, for example [40.jsonl:44](/workspace/logs/validation/40.jsonl:44), which repeatedly revisits the Massachusetts map question and never boxes an answer. Training's 4,096-token limit-hit rate rises from **0.78%** at step 1 to **5.37%** at step 40; its first-ten versus last-ten averages are **0.43% versus 4.67%**. Logged entropy falls from **0.4267 to 0.1257**, consistent with increasing concentration and repetitive behavior. Entropy is computed independently of the selected target IDs, so this remains useful observational evidence ([torch_functional.py:37](/workspace/framework/verl/utils/experimental/torch_functional.py:37)).
+
+The target defect establishes incorrect computation independently of these performance trends. The early validation improvement does not validate the implementation, and the later decline does not by itself diagnose it. The decline is consistent with corrupted policy updates, but this single sampled run cannot quantify the bug's causal contribution or exclude optimization effects from zero entropy regularization, no reference-KL penalty, and sparse mixed-group advantages.
+
+## Corrective Direction
+
+Before interpreting this recipe as a valid GRPO experiment, align fused targets with each local hidden-state shard: globally shift the unpadded IDs, apply the same padding and SP slicing, and consume those targets without shifting them again. The engine already constructs this tensor. Add an exact token-shape assertion in the fused head. Simply rolling an already sliced shard would introduce a boundary error. Disabling fused kernels consistently in the model and actor path is the immediate workaround because the non-fused engine uses the correct local targets. Verify fused/non-fused log-probability and gradient agreement under SP1 and SP2, including odd lengths and different packings. No training rerun was performed for this diagnosis.
*** End Patch"));

steps.message:
Wrote the diagnosis to [agent_answer.md](/logs/artifacts/agent_answer.md).

The run remains numerically stable, but fused log-probability computation uses incorrectly aligned targets under sequence parallelism, corrupting GRPO gradients. The report includes source evidence, a CPU reproduction, and a separate assessment of reward and validation trends. No additional training was run.
